reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: An acquired, often intensely pruritic eruption of discrete keratotic or crusted papules and papulovesicles on the trunk
Predominantly affects middle-aged and older men, particularly on the central chest and back
Frequently provoked by heat, sweating, sun exposure, prolonged bed rest, and febrile illness
Despite the name 'transient', a proportion of cases persist or relapse chronically
Histology shows focal acantholysis with several possible patterns resembling Darier, Hailey-Hailey, pemphigus, or spongiotic disease
Direct immunofluorescence is negative, distinguishing it from the autoimmune pemphigus group
It is a benign condition, and management centres on itch control and avoidance of aggravating factors such as heat and sweating
reference.pathophysiology: Grover disease is characterised by focal acantholysis and dyskeratosis in the epidermis, producing small blisters and keratotic papules, but unlike pemphigus it is not autoantibody-mediated and direct immunofluorescence is negative. The precise cause is unknown; disruption of the stratum corneum barrier and eccrine duct occlusion related to heat, sweating, xerosis, and ultraviolet exposure are thought to trigger transient loss of keratinocyte cohesion. Occlusion, immobility, and systemic illness commonly precipitate flares, and associations with malignancy and other dermatoses have been reported, though the disorder is fundamentally benign.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy demonstrating focal acantholysis and dyskeratosis
Direct immunofluorescence (negative) to exclude autoimmune pemphigus
Review of precipitating factors such as heat, sweating, and immobilisation
Assessment of xerosis and coexisting dermatoses
Consideration of an underlying systemic illness or malignancy in atypical or refractory cases
Medication review for potential drug-related triggers
redFlags: Atypical, widespread, or refractory disease prompting consideration of an underlying malignancy
Severe intractable pruritus disturbing sleep and quality of life
Diagnostic uncertainty requiring exclusion of autoimmune blistering disease
reference.prognosis: Grover disease is benign and often self-limiting over weeks to months, though a subset follows a persistent or relapsing course; it does not scar and generally responds to symptomatic measures and avoidance of triggers.
pitfalls: Confusing it with an autoimmune pemphigus without performing direct immunofluorescence
Failing to advise avoidance of heat, sweating, and occlusion that drive flares
Overtreating a fundamentally benign, self-limiting condition
Missing an underlying systemic illness in atypical or persistent presentations
management: Advise avoidance of triggers such as heat, sweating, sun exposure, occlusion and prolonged bed rest
Use topical corticosteroids with emollients as first-line therapy for the eruption and pruritus, adding topical calcineurin inhibitors or a vitamin D analogue as adjuncts
Give oral antihistamines for itch and correct coexisting xerosis
Escalate refractory or extensive disease to phototherapy, a systemic retinoid such as acitretin, or a short course of systemic corticosteroid
Review medications for potential drug-related triggers
Consider evaluation for an underlying systemic illness or malignancy in atypical or persistently refractory cases
